qwen.ref_text: On the battlefield, four players with monster-like strength appeared. Each of the players had already destroyed their colonies. These players were so equally strong, they created a four-way deadlock.

lines: Lecture eleven. Distributed machine learning. How many machines share the work of training one model.
First, push. Machine A sends its seven to machine B. That takes one message.
Push: A sends its 7 to B. One message.
Next, pull. B asks first, and then A replies. That takes two messages.
Pull: B asks first, then A replies. Two messages.
With a broadcast, A sends the same fifty megabyte model to four machines.
Broadcast: A sends the same 50 MB model to four machines.
So four copies leave A. Four times fifty is two hundred megabytes.
Four copies leave A: 4 × 50 = 200 MB.
Machines C one to C four each hold a number: three, five, two and six.
C1 to C4 each hold a number: 3, 5, 2 and 6.
A reduce adds them up as they arrive: three, eight, ten, sixteen.
Reduce sums them: 3, 8, 10, 16.
Only B gets the total of sixteen. That takes four messages.
Only B gets the total, 16. Four messages.
An all reduce adds up the same four numbers.
All-reduce sums the same four numbers.
Then sixteen goes back to every machine. That takes eight messages.
Then 16 goes back to every machine. Eight messages.
With a wait, B stops until the signal from A arrives.
Wait: B stops until A's signal arrives.
So B sat idle for six seconds.
B sat idle for 6 s.
With a barrier, nobody moves on until all four machines arrive.
Barrier: nobody goes on until all four arrive.
They all wait for the slowest one. In total, that is twelve seconds of idle machines.
They all wait for the slowest: 12 s of idle machines.
Each worker runs four rounds: three seconds of computing, then two seconds of sending.
Four rounds: 3 s of computing, then 2 s of sending.
With stop and wait, the worker sits still while it sends. It finishes after twenty seconds.
Stop and wait: the worker sits still while it sends. 20 s.
With overlap, it starts the next round while the last result is still being sent.
Overlap: start the next round while the last result is sent.
Now it is done in fourteen seconds. Six seconds of waiting are hidden.
Done in 14 s: 6 s of waiting is hidden.
Three workers each hold the same model, with w equal to ten.
Three workers, each with the same model, w = 10.
A minibatch of six examples is split, two examples per worker.
The minibatch of 6 is split: 2 examples per worker.
Each worker computes its own gradient: five, six and four.
Each worker computes its own gradient: 5, 6 and 4.
An all reduce adds them up, and a total of fifteen lands on every worker.
All-reduce: G = 15 lands on every worker.
Every copy makes the same update, so w becomes seven point five on all three.
Every copy updates the same way: w = 7.5.
That is exactly what one machine would get from all six examples. It is plain minibatch gradient descent.
Exactly what one machine gets from all 6: it is minibatch SGD.
Each iteration has three seconds of computing, then a one second all reduce.
Each iteration: 3 s of computing, then a 1 s all-reduce.
While the gradients travel, every worker waits.
While the gradients travel, every worker waits.
So the workers are computing only seventy-five percent of the time.
So the workers compute only 75% of the time.
Here are forty-five points and three starting centres.
45 points and 3 starting centres.
Each point joins its nearest centre, then each centre moves to the mean of its points.
Assign each point to the nearest centre, then move each centre to its mean.
Repeat. Some points switch cluster, and the centres follow them.
Repeat: points switch cluster and the centres follow.
At iteration six, no point switches, so k-means stops.
Iteration 6: no point switches, so k-means stops.
In map reduce, two mappers each get a copy of the centres, two and nine.
Two mappers get a copy of the centres, 2 and 9.
Each sample joins its nearest centre.
Each sample joins its nearest centre.
Sample eight is six away from c zero and one away from c one. So it emits the pair one, eight.
Sample 8: 6 from c0, 1 from c1, so it emits ⟨1, 8⟩.
Seven pairs go out. The key is the cluster, and the value is the sample.
7 pairs go out: the key is the cluster, the value the sample.
Here are the seven pairs from the map step, grouped by cluster.
The 7 pairs from the map step, grouped by cluster.
The combiner adds up each group as a sum and a count. Now there are four records instead of seven.
The combiner adds each group up: a sum and a count. 4 records instead of 7.
For cluster one, twenty plus fourteen, over two plus one, gives eleven point three three. That is the true mean.
Cluster 1: (20 + 14) ÷ (2 + 1) = 11.33, the true mean.
Averaging the local means would give twelve, because a mean forgets how many points it had.
Local means would give 12: a mean forgets how many points it had.
The reducer adds up the four records.
The reducer adds up the 4 records.
The new centres are ten over four, which is two point five, and thirty-four over three, which is eleven point three three.
The centres moved, so they go back to the mappers for another round.
The centres moved, so they go back to the mappers.
In the next round, no point changes cluster.
Next round: no point changes cluster.
The reducer's test says converged, and the job is done.
The reducer's test says converged: done.
An all reduce gives every machine the same total.
Waiting machines are wasted, so overlap computing with sending.
K-means runs as map reduce: assign in the map, add up sums and counts, then find the new means.
